name: ground_c
prompt:
Two images are attached. The first is a layout: 12 equal squares in a 4×3 grid on a flat magenta background. The second shows finished art from the same top-down 2D city game: roofs and cars, and on the right a square of the game's grass. Match that art's look: crisp hand-painted game art, clean confident brushwork, every small shape sharp and readable, natural colours. It must NOT look like a photograph: no blur, no photographic noise, no fine speckle mush.

Make one image with exactly the same 4×3 layout as the first image. Fill each square with the patch of ground described for that cell below: a ground texture the game repeats over large areas under the roofs and cars.

Shape comes first:
- Each square is filled edge to edge, right into all four corners, and stops exactly at its outline. Paint over the outline itself: the finished square has no border, frame, rim, bevel, outline, shadow or vignette, and its edges are as bright and as busy as its middle.
- Draw nothing outside the squares. Outside them, keep the background fully transparent. No text, numbers, labels or grid lines anywhere.

How each square is built: a calm, smooth painted base with gentle broad variation in its tone, and on it, scattered at random and spaced apart, distinct readable painted details — small stones, chips, stains, spots — each crisp-edged, with plenty of calm base between them. Not a uniform noise of tiny specks.

Rules for every cell:
- Look straight down (orthographic). No perspective, no light falling off towards any edge.
- Each square is 9.2 × 9.2 m of ground. Keep everything true to size: a stone in asphalt a centimetre or two, a crack no longer than a hand, a stain at most half a metre.
- No direction and no pattern at all: no joints, slabs, tiles, seams, lines, stripes, grooves or grid of any kind, no brush strokes running one way. Details scattered at random, so the square looks the same turned any way.
- Even texture: the same tone and the same density of detail all over the square, with no single feature bigger or darker than the rest, so it repeats without anything catching the eye.
- Squares that share a description are the same ground: draw them in exactly the same colours, density and style, as different patches of one surface, so they can be joined without a visible seam.
- Nothing stands on the ground and nothing is painted on it: no paint, road markings, lines, kerbs, manholes, drains, litter or objects.

Cells, left to right, top to bottom:

Row 1 — cells 1 and 2: a road's fresh asphalt: a smooth dark charcoal grey base, an even scatter of small crisp grey and pale stones.
Row 1 — cells 3 and 4: a road's worn asphalt: the same, a shade lighter and greyer, stones more exposed, a few tiny dark oil spots and hairline cracks no longer than a hand.

Row 2 — cells 5 and 6: a town pavement of poured concrete in one continuous surface: a smooth light warm grey base, a fine scatter of small pale and dark aggregate specks. No slabs and no joints.
Row 2 — cells 7 and 8: the same pavement weathered: a shade darker, soft grime stains, tiny chips and a few small dark gum spots. No slabs and no joints.

Row 3 — cells 9 and 10: a bridge deck's smooth cast concrete: a mid grey base, slightly darker and cooler than row 2, soft pale water stains.
Row 3 — cells 11 and 12: the same bridge concrete older: slightly darker, small pits, a few rust-brown drip stains and tiny hairline cracks.
